chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-A'ala ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), 'Does the fasting person smell the rose (aroma) and the perfume?' He said: 'There is no problem with it.' And it is reported that he did not smell the rose because it is disliked for him to derive pleasure from it.

key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no problem with it (permissible)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible for a fasting person to smell perfume or rose in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In *Al-Kafi*, Shaykh al-Kulayni records this narration to clarify the permissibility of smelling perfume during fasting, a common concern given that scent can trigger the sensation of taste. The primary ruling establishes general permissibility, while the secondary report introduces the principle of *karahah* (dislike) specifically when the scent induces pleasure (*talazzud*) that might lead to swallowing saliva or breaking the fast, reflecting the Shia juristic focus on preventing accidental nullification.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Muhammad Bin Al Husayn, from Ali Bin Al Hakam, from Al A’ala Bin Razeyn, from Muhammad Bin Muslim who said,

‘I said to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, ‘The Fasting one smells the aroma and the perfume. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘There is no problem with it’.
And it is reported that he<sup>asws</sup> did not smell the aromas because it was disliked for him<sup>asws</sup> that he<sup>asws</sup> derive pleasure with it.
en.sarwar: 4. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Hassan, from Ali ibn al-Hakam from al-‘Ala’ ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim who has said the following:

“I once asked abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, ’Can a fasting person smell sweet basil and perfumes?’ He (the Imam) said, ‘It is not harmful.’” It is narrated that he (the Imam) would not smell sweet basil because of his dislike to enjoy such pleasure.
